cues.text: The Legacy of Boniface VIII's Conflict with France
The Avignon Papacy had its roots in the bruising conflict between Pope Boniface VIII and King Philip IV of France .
The conflict climaxed in 1303, when French agents seized and assaulted the elderly pope at Anagni, hastening his death weeks later.
The episode left the papacy badly shaken and acutely aware of French royal power.
The Election of Clement V
In 1305 the College of Cardinals, under heavy French influence, elected the Gascon archbishop Bertrand de Got as Pope Clement V .
Crowned at Lyons in the presence of Philip IV, Clement chose not to travel to a Rome then wracked by aristocratic faction-fighting.
After several years moving between French cities, he settled the papal court at Avignon in 1309, a town within territory subject to papal overlordship since 1228.
Pressure from the French Crown
Clement's dependence on Philip IV had grave consequences.
Under royal pressure, he suppressed the Knights Templar in 1312 on charges of heresy that historians now widely regard as engineered for the French crown's financial benefit.
He also came under continual pressure to condemn the memory of his predecessor Boniface VIII.
Seven Avignon Popes

Clement V was followed by six more popes — John XXII, Benedict XII, Clement VI, Innocent VI, Urban V, and Gregory XI — all Frenchmen, who together governed the Church from Avignon for nearly seventy years.

The popes built the massive Palace of the Popes there, and the Avignon court, for all its administrative efficiency, became notorious among contemporaries for its opulence and its concentration of Church revenue and patronage in French hands.
Voices for Return
Critics, including St. Bridget of Sweden and St. Catherine of Siena, pressed urgently for the popes to return to Rome, the traditional see of St. Peter.

They framed the Avignon sojourn as a scandalous captivity—the phrase ‘Babylonian Captivity,’ comparing it to Israel’s exile in Babylon, entered common use in this period, popularized by the poet Petrarch.
Urban V briefly returned to Rome in 1367 but retreated to Avignon under cardinals' pressure three years later.
Legacy: End at Rome, Beginning of Deeper Crisis
Gregory XI, moved by these appeals, finally returned the papacy to Rome in January 1377, ending the Avignon period.
His death the following year, however, triggered the disputed election of Urban VI and the resulting Western Schism .
Rival popes at Rome and Avignon divided Christendom's obedience for nearly forty years.
This was a still deeper crisis for which the Avignon interlude had, in many ways, prepared the ground.
